Chapter 3: Learning to Love Yourself—The Foundation for Healthy Relationships.
In the quiet space of the meantime, a question starts to surface: what does it really mean to love yourself? For a lot of us, that idea feels a little strange, maybe even selfish. After years of chasing approval from parents, partners, or friends, it’s easy to lose touch with what we actually want or need.
But here’s the thing—the meantime, with its gentle push toward reflection, shows us that self-love isn’t some luxury or afterthought. It’s the bedrock for every healthy relationship that comes next.
Think about a young professional, always working overtime, eager to please her boss and keep her colleagues happy. Eventually, she hits a wall—exhausted, frustrated, and wondering why she always feels so empty. In her personal life, it’s the same story: she’s constantly giving, hoping someone will finally notice her worth.
But when the noise fades and she’s left with herself, something shifts. She starts to ask, “What do I really want?” And the answers surprise her. She craves rest, creativity, maybe even a little solitude. For the first time, she lets herself say no. She draws boundaries. She treats herself with the care and kindness she’s always saved for everyone else.
Most of us don’t even realize how harshly we talk to ourselves. That inner critic is always there, reminding us of every little flaw and mistake. And in the meantime, those voices can get even louder. But here’s the opportunity: you can start to challenge them. You can swap out self-judgment for self-compassion, seeing mistakes not as proof you’re unworthy, but as a natural part of being human.
Self-love isn’t about being perfect or always happy. It’s about accepting every part of who you are—the strengths and the struggles, the beautiful and the messy. It’s realizing that your worth isn’t something you have to earn. It’s already there.
And when you start treating yourself with respect and care, you’ll notice everything around you begins to shift. The relationships you attract start to reflect this new sense of value.
Take a man who’s spent years bouncing from one failed relationship to another, always searching for someone to fill the emptiness inside. He wants a partner to complete him, to fix what he thinks is broken. But in the meantime, he discovers something powerful: no one else can do that work for him. So he invests in his own growth—reading, learning, diving into new interests. And little by little, that desperate need for validation starts to fade. He finds joy in his own company, and the fear of being alone loses its grip.
For some, spirituality becomes part of this journey. Maybe it’s prayer, meditation, or just feeling connected to something bigger than themselves. There’s a sense that self-love isn’t just about the self—it’s a way of honoring the very life you’ve been given. The meantime turns into a sacred space, nourishing your soul and preparing your heart for deeper connection.
As your self-love grows, you’ll notice your ability to love others grows too. Those old patterns—neediness, trying to control, sacrificing yourself—start to fade away. Relationships stop being about filling a void. Instead, they become about sharing joy, growth, and real respect.
So, what once felt like a lonely stretch—the meantime—actually becomes the birthplace of true intimacy. First with yourself, and then, when the time is right, with someone else.
